title: OSI Model — Overview
html:
Open Systems Interconnection: the standard mental map for every layer of networking, top to bottom.

Definition

The OSI model is a conceptual, standardized framework that describes how data moves through a network in 7 distinct layers, each with a specific responsibility. It's "open" because it's vendor-neutral — any system following it can interoperate with any other.

Data physically only exists as electrical/light/radio signals — the OSI model is the human-friendly abstraction layered on top so engineers can reason about "what's happening" without tracking every electron. Each layer talks logically to its counterpart layer on the other machine, but physically only ever talks to the layer directly above/below it on the same machine.

L7
Application

What the user-facing software does

L6
Presentation

Formatting, encryption, translation

L5
Session

Setting up & managing connections

L4
Transport

TCP/UDP, segmentation, ports

L3
Network

IP addressing, routing

L2
Data Link

MAC addresses, framing

L1
Physical

Raw bits as electrical/light signals

Memory aid

A classic mnemonic, top-down: All People Seem To Need Data Processing — Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.

You ↔ Friend — the whole stack in one picture

Think of two people (computers) wanting to talk. On your side, data goes down the stack (A→P→S→T→N→D2→Physical), gets physically transmitted, and on the friend's side it goes back up the stack in reverse. Each layer adds its own header as data descends (this is called encapsulation), and each corresponding layer strips its header back off as data ascends on the receiving side (decapsulation).
